task_title: Loss of Control and Stall and Spin Awareness
area: Area VI. Safety and Risk Management
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a wing stalls and what raises stall speed, spot the base-to-final, go-around, departure and distraction traps that lead to loss of control, and talk through the recovery from a stall, spin, spiral dive or upset in the right order.
why: Loss of control in flight (LOC-I) is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents in the U.S. [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and it heads the FAA list of fatal GA accident causes for 2001 to 2016 [[30:21|RMH 3-3]]. Most stall and spin accidents start when the pilot is distracted for a moment from flying the airplane [[13:4|AC 61-67C par 3]]. The skills that prevent and fix an upset fade without practice, so they need regular refreshing [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

prereading.what: What loss of control and an upset are, the four groups of causes, task saturation, and surprise and startle.
prereading.label: AFH 5-1 to 5-3

prereading.what: Angle of attack, stall recognition, AOA indicators, stall characteristics and the six-step stall recovery template.
prereading.label: AFH 5-9 to 5-16

prereading.what: Turning, power-on, secondary, accelerated, cross-control and elevator trim stalls, and the common errors list.
prereading.label: AFH 5-18 to 5-21

prereading.what: Spin awareness, the spin phases, the spin recovery template, placarded airplanes and spiral dive recovery.
prereading.label: AFH 5-22 to 5-27

prereading.what: The FAA's stall and spin ground training: what changes stall speed, distractions, contamination, stall types and spin recovery.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C ch 1

prereading.what: Critical AOA, AOA indicators, load factor in turns and how it raises stall speed.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-36

prereading.what: Go-around power, attitude and configuration, and the turn back after an engine failure on takeoff.
prereading.label: AFH 9-11 and 18-7

warmup: Think first: You are turning base to final with a strong tailwind on base, and you see you will overshoot the centerline. Your hands want more bank and your foot wants more inside rudder. What is happening to your angle of attack and your stall speed, which way would the airplane spin if it stalled right now, and what is the safest fix?

key_terms.def: The angle at which the wing's chord line meets the relative wind.
The AOA where airflow separates from the top of the wing and it stalls. For a given configuration it does not change with weight, bank or density altitude.
Loss of lift when the critical AOA is exceeded. It can happen at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
The AOA has set off a stall warning but has not yet reached the critical AOA.
Lift divided by the airplane's weight, stated in G. A level 60 degree bank is 2 G.
A stall at more than 1 G, so it comes at a higher airspeed than the published stall speed.
A stall with aileron pushed one way and rudder the other, as in a skidding base-to-final turn.
A second stall caused by pulling up too soon or too hard while recovering from the first.
An aggravated stall with autorotation: the airplane corkscrews down with at least one wing stalled.
A steep, nose-low descending turn that is not stalled; airspeed and G load build fast.
An unintended state past normal limits: more than 25 degrees nose up, 10 degrees nose down, 45 degrees of bank, or a wrong airspeed for the conditions.
Do not use full or abrupt control movements at or above it. It goes down as weight goes down.

chunks.title: Loss of control: what it is and why it kills

body.p: LOC-I covers any significant departure from the intended flightpath, and it often follows an airplane upset. It is the leading cause of fatal general aviation accidents in the U.S. Maneuvering is the most common phase of flight for GA loss of control accidents, but they happen in every phase [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]. The RMH list of fatal GA accident causes for 2001 to 2016 puts LOC-I first [[30:21|RMH 3-3]], and its glossary notes that many LOC-I accidents are the result of stalls, spins or accelerated maneuvers [[30:74|RMH G-2]].

head: An upset is any unintended
Value [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]
rows: Inappropriate for the conditions, even inside the limits above (this includes stalls)

body.p: The AFH lists the situations that raise the risk: uncoordinated flight, equipment malfunctions, complacency, distraction, turbulence and poor risk management. Its common example of poor risk management is trying to fly in IMC without being qualified or proficient [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]. It groups the causes of upsets that led to LOC-I accidents as environmental, mechanical, human and stall-related factors [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

bullets: Environmental: turbulence, mountain waves, wind shear, thunderstorms, wake turbulence from other aircraft, and icing [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Mechanical: asymmetrical flaps, binding flight controls, runaway trim, or a malfunctioning or misused autopilot [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

Human: VMC into IMC, diversion of attention, task saturation, sensory overload, spatial disorientation, surprise and startle [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Many upsets start while the pilot is busy with a task that pulls the eyes off the instruments and the outside view [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

An upset is not the same as an unusual attitude drill. It includes stalls and overspeeds, it is unintended, and it can bring startle. A 30 degree bank with 15 degrees nose up set by an instructor is an unusual attitude, not an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

body.p: The PHAK adds a number worth remembering: more than 25 percent of GA fatal accidents happen in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve stall or spin scenarios [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

callout.text: Prevention happens on two time scales. Planning and risk management work over minutes or hours; a proportional control response to a developing upset works in seconds or less [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

check.q: Which phase of flight is the most common for GA loss of control accidents?
check.a: Maneuvering, though LOC-I accidents happen in every phase [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

chunks.title: Angle of attack and the stall

body.p: Angle of attack is the angle at which the wing's chord meets the relative wind. As AOA grows, lift and drag grow. Above the wing's critical AOA, the airflow separates from the upper surface, lift drops and drag rises. That is a stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

callout.text: A stall is about angle of attack, not airspeed. You can exceed the critical AOA at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

body.p: The critical AOA is roughly 16 to 20 degrees depending on the design, and each airplane stalls at its own one AOA whatever the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. For a given configuration it does not change with weight, bank angle, temperature, density altitude or CG [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]]. A stalled wing still makes some lift; it just cannot make enough for level flight [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

Most training airplanes are built so the wing root stalls first, which leaves the ailerons some effect at the stall. That is no license to use them first. If the airplane rolls left at the stall and you add right aileron, the down aileron raises the left wing's AOA, the tip stalls more fully, and the roll can get worse. Reduce AOA before you roll [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

head: Level
What it means [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]
rows: The AOA sets off a stall warning but has not reached the critical AOA. Cues: buffet, stick shaker or aural warning.
The critical AOA is exceeded. Usually an uncommanded nose-down pitch you cannot readily stop, sometimes with an uncommanded roll.

check.q: Your airplane stalls at about 17 degrees AOA in level flight at gross weight. Same flaps, but now in a steep turn at a lighter weight. What is the critical AOA?
check.a: The same. For a given configuration it does not change with weight or bank [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]]; only the airspeed at which you reach it changes.

body.p: The level-flight stall speed in the POH holds only in unaccelerated 1 G flight, in coordinated flight, at one weight (typically maximum gross) and at one CG (typically the forward limit) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of those and the stall speed changes.

head: Factor
Effect on stall speed
rows: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]]. A level coordinated 60 degree bank is 2 G and the stall comes 41 percent above the 1 G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
Heavier means a higher stall speed, because the wing needs more AOA to carry the weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100i]].

A forward CG often makes the wing reach the stalling AOA at a higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100h]]. An aft CG takes less elevator force to stall, which makes an inadvertent stall easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100h]].
Extending flaps generally lowers the stall speed. That is why the bottom of the white arc is below the bottom of the green arc [[13:7|AC 61-67C par 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100c]].

Even a small amount raises the stall speed; do not attempt flight with it on the airplane [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100k]]. With ice the airplane may stall at much higher speeds and lower AOA than normal [[28:249|AWH 20.3.10]].
A vertical gust or wind shear can raise the AOA suddenly, so the stall can come at a much higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]].
Little or no effect on indicated stall speed. Fly the same indicated approach speeds at a high density altitude airport [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100j]].

body.p: Why does bank raise the stall speed? In a level turn the wing must lift the weight plus the load from the turn, so you add back pressure and the AOA rises as the bank increases. If the AOA becomes excessive at any point in the turn, the airplane stalls [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. The curve stays flat at shallow banks and then climbs fast. Load factor rises at a terrific rate past about 45 or 50 degrees of bank [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and the stall speed is up by about one-half at a bank of about 63 degrees [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. AC 61-67C gives the classic example: an airplane that stalls at 45 knots unaccelerated can be stalled at 90 knots at 4 G [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]].

callout.text: Structure is a limit too. Do not use full or abrupt control movements at or above VA, and large alternating inputs can overstress the airplane even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100f]]. Maneuvering speed is lower at a lower weight [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]].

Icing and structural ice are covered in RF.VI.A. For this lesson, remember that contamination can take away the usual stall cues and that the stall may come well above the normal stall speed [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102a, b]].

check.q: Your POH lists one stall speed for flaps up. Name two things that make it the wrong number today.
check.a: Any of these: more than 1 G (a bank or a pull), a slip or skid, a weight or CG different from the one it was measured at [[24:118|AFH 5-13]], or frost or ice on the wing [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100k]].

bullets: Feel: control pressures get lighter, you need bigger movements for the same response, and the airplane answers more slowly [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Sound: the noise of the air along the airplane changes as speed drops [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Vision: useful for pitch awareness, but not a sure cue, since you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Kinesthesia, the seat-of-the-pants sense of changes in speed and direction, can warn a trained pilot [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Mushy controls, a loss of rpm in a fixed-pitch airplane approaching a power-on stall, then buffeting or vibration just before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].
Stall warning devices on many aircraft sound 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 103]].

body.p: Not every airplane has a warning device. Most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have none and rely on pre-stall buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. A warning system can also fail, so use the other cues: buffet, loss of roll authority, or not being able to stop a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. In a power-off stall the buffet is less noticeable than in a power-on stall; the main cue may be the elevator against its stop and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

An AOA indicator shows the margin between your AOA and the critical AOA. The FAA and the GA Joint Steering Committee promote them to cut loss of control accidents [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Their limits include calibration, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:119|AFH 5-14]]. If your airplane has one, learn how it works and practice with it in slow flight, stalls, takeoffs and landings [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

callout.text: Recognition should trigger a reflex. The most important action for an impending stall or a full stall is to reduce the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: In a power-off stall with the buffet barely noticeable, what may be the main cue?
check.a: The elevator control full back against the stops and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: The AFH describes the classic setup for a skidding cross-control stall. A tailwind component on base, not noticed, gives a higher groundspeed. The pilot turns late or too shallow and overshoots the centerline. To fix it, the pilot steepens the bank, pulls, and pushes inside rudder to swing the nose around. The bank tends to increase and the nose drops, so the pilot pulls harder, moving the AOA toward critical. A stall with these inputs can become a spin very quickly [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: A spin from a cross-controlled stall usually turns in the direction of the rudder being applied, whichever wingtip is raised. In a slipping turn, with opposite aileron held against the rudder, the spin usually goes opposite to the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

body.p: AC 61-67C names three power-off traps that have caused many stall and spin accidents: crossed-control turns from base to final, trying to stop a high sink rate on final by pitch alone, and poor airspeed control in the pattern [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104a]]. In uncoordinated flight the airspeed indicator and altimeter can read wrong, so the stall warning may be your first clue [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

callout.text: The safest fix for an overshoot is a go-around. Low in the pattern, be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees of bank, and never skid to correct an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Correct for wind on downwind and base so the final turn is normal. Inadequate wind drift correction on base and an overshooting turn are listed landing errors [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Keep the ball centered. A skidding turn from base to final and poor coordination in that turn are on the same list [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Do not try to reach the runway with elevator alone [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]; use power.

check.q: In an overshooting left turn to final you hold left rudder and right aileron, and the airplane stalls. Which way is it likely to spin?
check.a: Left, the way the rudder is applied, whichever wingtip is raised [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

body.p: Power-on stalls cause many accidents during takeoff and climbout, particularly in go-arounds. AC 61-67C names a nose-high trim setting and premature flap retraction as causal factors [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 104b]]. High pitch, high power and low airspeed also mean strong left yaw from P-factor; too little or too much rudder leaves you uncoordinated near the critical AOA [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]].

A go-around has three cardinal principles: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The trim is set for a slow approach, so full power makes the nose rise and the airplane yaw left. Letting the nose rise too early can cause an unrecoverable stall at low altitude. Expect to need considerable forward pressure and right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. If full power brings high control pressures, use caution reaching for the flap handle; airplane control comes first [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Raise the flaps only after the descent is stopped, partly or to the takeoff setting, in small steps as the airplane accelerates. A sudden full retraction can cost enough lift to settle the airplane into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delays in going around come from landing expectancy and from pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Departure has its own trap. If the engine fails in the climb, straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk choice. Turning back without training needs considerable luck, and if the nose is not lowered enough during the turn an accelerated stall may follow [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. In the AFH example, the engine quits at 300 ft AGL; after a 4 second reaction, a standard-rate turn of 225 degrees takes 75 seconds, and at about 1,000 fpm the airplane ends up 1,016 ft below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

callout.text: Airspeed decays very quickly when the power quits in a climb attitude. AC 61-67C uses a gliding turn demonstration to show the altitude loss and why returning to the airport after losing the engine is not recommended [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200c]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C par 200c]]. A turn back is only for a trained pilot who knows the airplane can make it [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

body.p: At night or with no horizon, the strong acceleration of a takeoff can feel like a nose-up pitch, and the disoriented pilot pushes into a nose-low attitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]]. Fly the attitude indicator.

check.q: Full flaps, nose-up trim, and you add full power to go around. What will the airplane try to do, and what do you do?
check.a: Pitch up sharply and yaw left. Hold forward pressure and right rudder, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

body.p: AC 61-67C says stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with something else: finding a checklist, trying a restart after an engine failure, flying a pattern on a windy day, reading a chart, doing fuel or distance math, or reaching for something on the floor, in the back seat or in the glove box [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]]. The study behind the AC found stall and spin accidents were about one-quarter of fatal GA accidents, and NTSB data show most of them follow a momentary distraction [[13:4|AC 61-67C par 3]].

bullets: Diversion of attention: a malfunction, poor monitoring of automation, or just setting avionics can pull you off basic control [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Task saturation: the margin of safety is the gap between what the task demands and what you can do. An upset can follow whenever demands exceed capability [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Sensory overload: an upset can bring many visual, aural and touch warnings at once, while an expected warning may fail to come. Cross-check to sort what matters [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

Surprise and startle: surprise is an unexpected event that disrupts your thinking; startle is an automatic reflex with a jump in heart rate and blood pressure. Scenario training with realistic distractions builds protection [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

body.p: Automation can hide the cues. An autopilot may mask the feel of an approaching stall or try to fly the airplane in the stall, and a sudden disconnect with the trim at an extreme setting makes recovery harder [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102c]]. That is why disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot is step one of the stall recovery template [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

callout.text: Application: before you reach for anything, set the attitude and trim, then do the task in short looks with the scan going. AC 61-67C's list of training distractions (dropping a pencil, reading a chart, calling for weather) is a good list of moments to be careful [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200a(10)]].

check.q: Name three tasks AC 61-67C links to inadvertent stalls.
check.a: Any three of: locating a checklist, an engine restart attempt, a windy-day pattern, reading a chart, fuel or distance calculations, retrieving items from the floor, back seat or glove compartment [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]].

chunks.title: Low, steep and slow: the maneuvering trap

body.p: The RMH tells of a pilot who buzzes friends at a park. The airplane does not climb as he expected, he pulls hard, the airspeed drops, and the airplane is close to stalling as the wing brushes a power line. The RMH uses him to show the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes: macho (taking chances is foolish), anti-authority (follow the rules), invulnerability (it could happen to me), impulsivity (not so fast, think first) and resignation (I can make a difference) [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].

Low and steep is where load factor kills. A sudden loss of control in a steep turn, or an abrupt pull on the elevator near the ground, has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Knowing load factors and VA helps prevent stalls from steep turns or excessive maneuvering near the ground [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The AFH adds that unnecessary low flying and impromptu demonstrations for people on the ground can push pilots past their capabilities, with fatal results [[24:108|AFH 5-3]], and asks pilots to look for flights that could involve low-altitude maneuvering, steep turns in the pattern, uncoordinated flight or high load factors [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

callout.text: 91.119: except when necessary for takeoff or landing, fly no lower than an altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard if the engine fails; over congested areas, 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft; elsewhere, 500 ft above the surface, and over open water or sparsely populated areas no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

91.307(c): carrying anyone other than a crewmember, you may not make an intentional maneuver past 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose up or nose down unless each occupant wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. The exceptions are flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. 91.303 bars aerobatic flight below 1,500 ft above the surface, over congested areas and in some airspace [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

body.p: Slow makes it worse. In slow flight, turns need more power to hold altitude, and abrupt or rough control movements may stall the airplane [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Gusts can stall the airplane while you fight to hold the flightpath, so in moderate or severe turbulence or strong crosswinds AC 61-67C calls for a higher than normal approach speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100l]]. Thunderstorm gusts can be strong enough to stall an aircraft even at maneuvering speed [[28:235|AWH 19.2.1.1]], and a microburst tailwind shear on approach can cause a stall or a landing short [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

callout.text: Application: near the ground, the urge to pull to clear an obstacle is strongest exactly when the AOA has the least margin. Pulling harder past the critical AOA only deepens the stall [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: A non-crew friend on board, no parachutes. May you fly a 65 degree bank over their house for photos?
check.a: No. 91.307(c) bars intentional banks past 60 degrees with a non-crew occupant unless everyone wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]], and 91.119 sets your minimum altitude [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

chunks.title: Stall recovery: reduce the angle of attack first

body.p: Whatever the airplane, the most important action for an impending or full stall is to reduce the AOA. The AFH notes many accidents where pilots tried to fix the stall with power and by holding altitude instead, and lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Follow the manufacturer's procedure if one is published and current [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

head: Step
What and why [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
rows: Manual control is essential; the autopilot may make control or trim changes you will not notice.
Push until the impending stall indications are gone, before going on. Too much trim can make things worse.
Points the lift vector the right way. Do not try to control bank before reducing AOA; use rudder to stop yaw so the stall does not become a spin.
Power reduces the altitude lost but does not eliminate a stall. AOA reduction is what breaks it.
Smooth and coordinated, avoiding a secondary stall and watching the terrain.

body.p: In a single-engine trainer without an autopilot or speed brakes, that leaves four steps: reduce AOA until the warning stops, roll wings level, add power as needed, and return to the desired flightpath, all coordinated [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

bullets: Do not overdo the push. Too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by putting a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]], and low or negative G is a listed recovery error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Secondary stall: it comes from pulling the nose up too soon or too hard, or from trying to break a stall with power only. Recover the same way: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinate, adjust power [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Accelerated stall: it comes above the 1 G stall speed and tends to be more aggressive; if uncoordinated, the bank may change. Same recovery, right away [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Contaminated wing: the AOA must come down at once, with aggressive power, and do not return to the AOA or airspeed at which the upset began [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102b]].

callout.text: Practice stalls high enough to recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL in a single-engine airplane, or higher if the AFM or POH says so [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[13:15|AC 61-67C par 200]].

check.q: In a full stall the left wing drops sharply. What is your first control action?
check.a: Nose-down pitch to reduce the AOA until the stall warning stops, then roll wings level [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Aileron first can deepen the stall on the low wing [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

body.p: A spin needs two things: a stall and yaw. At least one wing is stalled, and the airplane descends in a corkscrew [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA with too much or too little rudder, and to a lesser extent aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C par 109]]. Keeping the nose from yawing before you start the stall recovery is the key to avoiding one [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

The four phases are entry, incipient, developed and recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Start recovery from an incipient spin before 360 degrees of rotation. Find the direction from the turn indicator's symbolic airplane, not from the ball, which moves according to where it is mounted [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

bullets: Power to idle: power flattens the spin and usually speeds the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
Ailerons neutral: aileron either way can steepen, flatten or delay the recovery [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

Full opposite rudder, briskly, held until the rotation stops. Rudder tends to be the most important recovery control in typical single-engine airplanes, and slow, cautious rudder can let the spin go on [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].
Brisk forward elevator, right after the rudder; do not wait for the rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].
Neutralize the rudder when the rotation stops, then pull back smoothly, avoiding a secondary stall and G or airspeed limits [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].
These are generic steps. The manufacturer's procedure comes first [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

head: Problem
How it looks
Recovery in short
rows: Stalled; airspeed low and steady; rotating [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Idle, ailerons neutral, opposite rudder, forward elevator, neutral rudder, smooth pull [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Not stalled; steep nose-low turn; airspeed and G rising fast [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Idle, some forward elevator to unload to about 1 G, roll wings level, gently raise the nose, then climb power at VY [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Pitch or bank past the upset limits [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]
Disconnect autopilot, push to unload, roll to the nearest horizon, adjust power by airspeed, return to level flight [[24:111|AFH 5-6]]

body.p: Upsets start with recognition. Any time the view outside or the instruments differ from what you expect, assume an upset and cross-check to confirm the attitude or find a failed instrument [[24:110|AFH 5-5]]. The AFH lists the common upset recovery errors: misjudging the kind of upset, not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, not unloading when needed, rolling the wrong way, and poor airspeed management [[24:112|AFH 5-7]]. Upset training in an airplane is limited by the maneuvers that airplane is approved for and by the instructor's own UPRT skill [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

callout.text: In a spiral dive, pulling back while rolling to wings level (a rolling pullout) can exceed the design limit. Unload first, then roll, then raise the nose gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. If the airspeed is increasing, you are no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

You must comply with the operating limitations, markings and placards in the approved flight manual [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]. Normal category airplanes are placarded against intentional spins; they were tested only for a one-turn or 3-second spin [[13:21|AC 61-67C par 400a]]. In an airplane placarded against spins there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

body.p: Spins eat altitude: about 1,000 ft for the first turn and about half that for each turn after [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. In a constant turn with no horizon, the graveyard spiral illusion makes a descending turn feel wings level, and the pilot who pulls back only tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5b]].

check.q: Why move the elevator forward right after full opposite rudder instead of waiting for the rotation to stop?
check.a: The AFH says not to wait. The forward elevator reduces AOA and drives the airplane toward unstalled flight [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

bullets: Treating the published stall speed as fixed. Fix: it holds only at 1 G, coordinated, at one weight and CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Leveling the wings or adding power before reducing AOA. Fix: nose down first [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Not holding the nose-down input until the stall warning stops. Fix: hold it, then roll level [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Pulling up abruptly after the recovery. Fix: smooth return; a secondary stall is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Skidding to tighten a final turn. Fix: no more than 30 degrees of bank low, and go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Letting the nose rise and raising all the flaps at once on a go-around. Fix: forward pressure, right rudder, flaps up in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Slow or cautious rudder in a spin recovery, or waiting for the rotation to stop before moving the elevator forward. Fix: brisk full rudder, then forward elevator [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
Adding power or pulling while rolling in a spiral. Fix: power idle, unload, roll, then raise the nose [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

check.q: Which listed spiral dive recovery error comes first on the AFH list?

scenario.title: A lake tour with a friend
scenario.setup: You are flying again after two years away. On a calm Sunday you take one friend, who is not a pilot, on a tour of a lake in a narrow valley. The rented four-seat single is placarded against intentional spins. Your friend's family has a cabin on the shore, with a dock and a few boats. Your friend has a camera and plenty of requests.

questions.q: Your friend asks you to circle the cabin at about 300 ft above the water so the dock fills the photo. What do the rules say?
questions.a: 91.119 requires an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property, 500 ft above the surface away from congested areas, and over open water or sparsely populated areas no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. With a non-crew friend aboard and no parachutes, you also may not intentionally pass 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose up or down [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

questions.q: Even where it is legal, why is a low, slow, steep circle so dangerous?
questions.a: Bank adds load factor and raises the stall speed: 2 G and 41 percent more at a level 60 degree bank [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Sudden loss of control in a steep turn or an abrupt pull near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]], maneuvering is the most common phase for GA LOC-I [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and impromptu demonstrations for friends can push pilots past their capabilities [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

questions.q: At a safe height, your friend points at the cabin and you look out the side window for a long time. What does AC 61-67C warn about?
questions.a: Stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 101]]; identifying objects on the ground is one of the distractions the AC uses in training [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200a(10)]]. Application: set the attitude and keep the scan going between short looks.

questions.q: Circling at a safe height, you let the airspeed sag. The stall horn sounds, and the nose and left wing drop. Talk through the recovery.
questions.a: Push forward to reduce the AOA until the warning stops, then roll the wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, add power as needed, and return smoothly to the flightpath without a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Do not lead with aileron before the AOA is reduced [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

questions.q: Your friend has seen spins on video and asks for "just one turn." What do you say?
questions.a: No. You must comply with the placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]], and in an airplane placarded against spins there is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Normal category airplanes were tested only for a one-turn or 3-second spin [[13:21|AC 61-67C par 400a]].

questions.q: Before you fly friends again, what practice makes sense?
questions.a: Impending and full stalls with a CFI, high enough to recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], with realistic distractions such as reading a chart or identifying a landmark [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200a(10)]]. If the airplane has an AOA indicator, practice with it in slow flight, stalls, takeoffs and landings [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

skills.do: Given a stall, spin, spiral dive or nose-high or nose-low upset (what led to it, the attitude, and what the instruments show), say what the airplane is doing and talk through the recovery steps in order, explaining why AOA comes before roll and power in a stall, why power comes off first in a spin or spiral, and when the POH procedure overrides the generic template.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the three AFH templates aloud: stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], spin [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] and spiral [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Then fly impending and full power-on and power-off stalls with a CFI high enough to recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], adding realistic distractions from AC 61-67C [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200a(10)]]. For spins or all-attitude upset training, use an airplane approved for it and an instructor with that experience [[24:113|AFH 5-8]].

quiz.q: What range does the PHAK give for the critical AOA, depending on the design?
quiz.why: The critical AOA varies from about 16 to 20 degrees by design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: In a level, coordinated 60 degree bank, how much higher is the stall speed than the 1 G stall speed, per the AFH?
quiz.why: 60 degrees of bank is 2 G, and the stall comes 41 percent above the 1 G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what should you assume any time the view outside or the instruments differ from what you expect?
options: Instrument error, so ignore the gauges
An upset, then cross-check to confirm the attitude or a failed instrument
quiz.why: Assume an upset and cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or an instrument failure [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK say happens to lift when a wing stalls?
options: The wing still makes some lift, but not enough for level flight
Lift is unchanged; only drag rises
quiz.why: A stalled wing does not totally stop producing lift; it cannot make enough to sustain level flight [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: What are the go-around's three cardinal principles, in order?
What does adding power do in a stall recovery, according to the AFH?
options: It breaks the stall by itself
It reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate the stall
It should come before reducing AOA
quiz.why: Power typically reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; reducing AOA is imperative [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: Which control does the AFH call the most important for spin recovery in typical single-engine airplanes?
quiz.why: Rudder tends to be the most important recovery control, applied briskly and fully against the rotation [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

quiz.q: In the AFH upset recovery template, which way do you roll?
options: The way the nose is pointing
quiz.why: Step 3 is to roll the wings aggressively to the nearest horizon, after disconnecting the autopilot and unloading [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what two things usually delay a go-around?
quiz.why: Delay normally comes from landing expectancy (the belief the approach is sure to end well) and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You want upset training beyond stalls in your flying club's normal category trainer. What does the AFH say limits airplane-based UPRT?
options: The maneuvers the airplane is approved for and the instructor's own UPRT skill
Nothing; any airplane and any CFI will do
final_quiz.why: The level of upset training may be limited by the maneuvers approved for the airplane and by the instructor's UPRT capabilities [[24:112|AFH 5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Recovering from a practice stall, you shove the yoke so far forward that you float up off the seat. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; more push is always better
Too much forward pressure puts a negative load on the wing and can hinder the recovery
It causes a secondary stall from too much AOA
It means the stall was never broken
final_quiz.why: Too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by imposing a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]], and low or negative G is a listed recovery error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a practice aerobatic maneuver outside controlled airspace, over open fields, more than 4 nm from any airway, at 1,200 ft AGL with 5 sm visibility. Which 91.303 condition does it fail?
final_quiz.why: Aerobatic flight is not allowed below 1,500 ft above the surface [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

final_quiz.q: Your engine quits at 400 ft AGL after takeoff from an urban airport with hazards in the departure path. When does the AFH say a turn back might be made?
options: Whenever you are above 300 ft AGL
Only if you are certain the airplane can reach the field and you have trained and practiced the turn back
Any time there are hazards ahead
final_quiz.why: Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk option; with hazards ahead a pilot might turn back, but only if certain of reaching the field and trained and practiced in the maneuver [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: On a go-around in an airplane with heavy control pressures at full power, what does the AFH say about reaching for the flap handle?
options: Raise the flaps first, then fly
Use caution; airplane control is the first consideration
Have a passenger hold the yoke
Flaps are never touched during a go-around
final_quiz.why: On airplanes with high control pressures at maximum power, use caution reaching for the flap handle; airplane control comes first [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You have not flown for two years but practiced stalls a lot as a student. Why does the AFH say upset and stall skills need refreshing?
options: They are perishable and need continuous reinforcement
They do not need refreshing once learned
final_quiz.why: Upset prevention and recovery skills are perishable and need continuous reinforcement through training [[24:110|AFH 5-5]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

final_quiz.q: You fly into an airport at 7,000 ft density altitude. What indicated approach speed should you fly?
options: 5 knots slower to shorten the landing
final_quiz.why: Higher true airspeed at altitude does not change indicated stall or approach speeds; keep the manufacturer's indicated speeds [[13:9|AC 61-67C par 100j]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is a common upset recovery error listed in the AFH?
options: Failing to unload the airplane when needed
Adjusting power by watching the airspeed
final_quiz.why: The listed errors include failure to unload the airplane if necessary; the other choices are steps of the upset recovery template [[24:112|AFH 5-7]] [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

final_quiz.q: With ice on the wing, the airplane rolls off with little warning at an airspeed well above normal stall. What does AC 61-67C advise?
options: Hold altitude and add power slowly
Reduce pitch promptly to lower AOA, apply power aggressively, and stay away from the AOA where the upset began
Use full aileron against the roll first
final_quiz.why: Lower AOA at once with aggressive power, and do not return to the AOA or airspeed at which the upset happened [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102b]].

final_quiz.q: The AFH says LOC-I prevention works on two time scales. Which pairing is right?
options: ADM and risk management: minutes or hours; proportional counter-response: seconds or less
Both are done only before the flight
final_quiz.why: Prevention through ADM and risk management works over minutes or hours; proportional counter-response works over seconds or fractions of seconds [[24:111|AFH 5-6]].

final_quiz.q: Which does the AFH give as a common example of poor risk management that leads to LOC-I?
options: Trying to fly in IMC without being qualified or proficient
final_quiz.why: Attempting to fly in IMC when not qualified or proficient is the AFH's common example of poor risk management [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

final_quiz.q: Practicing slow flight with full flaps at a safe altitude, you suddenly raise the flaps all the way while holding altitude. What may happen?
options: Nothing; flaps do not affect the stall
The airplane may stall, because the stall speed rises as the flaps come up
The airplane will speed up and climb
final_quiz.why: Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]; flap extension lowers the stall speed, so taking them away raises it [[13:7|AC 61-67C par 100c]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot wants to buzz friends at a picnic "just this once" because nothing bad happened before. Which hazardous attitude and antidote fit best?
options: Resignation: I can make a difference
Invulnerability: it could happen to me
final_quiz.why: Thinking an accident won't happen because it hasn't before is invulnerability; the antidote is "It could happen to me" [[30:21|RMH 3-3]].

takeaways: A stall is about angle of attack, not airspeed: it can happen at any speed, attitude or power.
Stall speed rises with load factor (41 percent at a level 60 degree bank), weight, forward CG, contamination and gusts.
Low, steep and slow near the ground is the deadliest mix; respect 91.119 and 91.307 and skip the low pass.
Overshooting the final turn? Do not skid; keep the bank shallow and go around.
Go-around: power, attitude, configuration, with forward pressure and right rudder against the trim.
Stall recovery: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, power as needed, back to the flightpath.
Spin: idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, forward elevator. Spiral: idle, unload, roll level, then raise the nose.
cfi_notes: AC 61-67C gives the stall recovery as reduce AOA, then maximum allowable power, then straight and level with coordinated controls [[13:11|AC 61-67C par 105]]. The AFH template rolls the wings level before adding power as needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Both put AOA reduction first, and both defer to the manufacturer's procedure when one is published [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C par 111]].

Spin elevator timing: AC 61-67C says to move the elevator forward "when the rotation slows" [[13:13|AC 61-67C par 111]]; the AFH says to apply it right after full rudder and not to wait for the rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The POH procedure comes first in either case.

Spin altitude loss: AC 61-67C estimates about 500 ft per 3-second turn [[13:13|AC 61-67C par 111]]. The AFH text says about 1,000 ft for the first turn and about half that for each turn after, while AFH Figure 5-16 on the same page shows about 500 ft per 3-second turn and an incipient spin of about 2 turns [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; the next page says the incipient phase may take two to four turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Treat all of these as rough numbers.

AC 61-67C says a 60 degree bank raises stall speed 40 percent [[13:7|AC 61-67C par 100b]]; the AFH says 41 percent [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The square root of 2 is 1.414, a rise of 41.4 percent, so the two are the same figure rounded differently.

In the turn back example, the AFH text puts the airplane 4,200 ft to the side after the 180 degree turn [[24:356|AFH 18-7]], while Figure 18-5 is labeled 4,480 feet [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Both show the same 1,016 ft below the runway result.

AC 61-67C par 301 still reads that the 91.307 parachute exception covers an ATP instructing under 61.167 [[13:20|AC 61-67C par 301]], though its change page says that reference was removed [[13:1|AC 61-67C CHG 2]]. The current CFR text reads 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. Teach the CFR.

AC 61-67C chapter 4 describes spin certification under the old 23.221 [[13:21|AC 61-67C par 400a]]. The AFH notes 23.221(a) still applies to airplanes certified under it [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], while 23.2150 states current requirements, including that single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics must not tend to depart controlled flight inadvertently [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]].

Teaching tip: refresher pilots rarely need spins; spin training is required only for flight instructor applicants [[13:19|AC 61-67C par 300]]. Spend the time on recognition with realistic distractions [[13:16|AC 61-67C par 200a(10)]] and on chair-flying the templates. Make sure the pilot knows the cross-control and elevator trim stalls are demonstration maneuvers [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Interpretation: the AFH says untrained pilots often react to an upset with instinctive, abrupt control inputs [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. Application: ask the pilot to say each recovery step aloud during practice so the order becomes the reflex.
gaps: Stall speeds at various banks, weights and flap settings, stall characteristics, and the spin recovery procedure for a given airplane come from its POH or AFM, not these sources.
AC 61-67C asks for a higher than normal approach speed in turbulence or strong crosswinds but gives no amount; the POH or a CFI must supply it.
The AFH points to AC 120-109 and AC 120-111 for stall and upset training, but they are not in the source set, so their content is not taught here.
How a particular AOA indicator computes and shows AOA depends on the make; the AFH says to use its handbook or ask the manufacturer.
Turn back altitudes for a given make and model must be found in training with an instructor; the sources give only the method and an example.

activities.title: Read the bank angle chart
activities.intro: Drag each description to the pin it describes. Red is stall speed increase; black is load factor.

pins.label: 30 degrees, the most bank the AFH likes low in the pattern: stall speed up only about 7 percent
Level 60 degree bank: stall speed up about 41 percent
Level 60 degree bank: the wing carries 2 G
About 70 degrees: near 3 G and the yield point of the average light plane

activities.why: Application: in a level turn the load factor is 1 / cos(bank), so 30 degrees gives 1.155 G, and its square root, 1.075, means about 7 percent [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. The AFH says to be reluctant to use more than 30 degrees low in the pattern [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A level 60 degree bank is 2 G and a 41 percent rise [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Another 10 degrees adds about 1 G, near the yield point reached at about 70 to 75 degrees [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

activities.title: Legal under Part 91?
activities.intro: Tap each plan, then tap whether the rules allow it.

items.t: A non-crew friend aboard, no parachutes: a 45 degree bank to look at a lake
A non-crew friend aboard, no parachutes: a 70 degree bank to show how a steep turn feels
A non-crew friend aboard, no parachutes: pulling to 35 degrees nose up for fun
A non-crew friend aboard, no parachutes: a 25 degree nose-down attitude in a descent
A CFI giving a flight instructor applicant the required spin training, no parachutes
Aerobatics at 5,000 ft AGL within 4 nm of the centerline of a Federal airway
Solo over open, sparsely populated country, passing 300 ft from a farmhouse

activities.why: 91.307(c) limits intentional maneuvers with non-crew occupants to 60 degrees of bank and 30 degrees nose up or down unless everyone wears an approved parachute, and (d) exempts spins and other required maneuvers given by a CFI [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. 91.303 bars aerobatics within 4 nm of a Federal airway centerline [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. Over sparsely populated areas you may not fly closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]].

activities.title: True or false: upsets and their causes
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An instructor setting up a 30 degree bank with 15 degrees nose up has created an upset.
cards.why: False. That is an unusual attitude; an upset is unintended and past 45 degrees of bank, 25 up or 10 down, or a wrong airspeed [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:106|AFH 5-1]].

cards.s: Wake turbulence from another aircraft is one of the environmental causes of upsets.
Runaway trim and binding flight controls are human factors.
Upset prevention and recovery training is the same thing as aerobatic training.
cards.why: False. In aerobatic training the pilot expects the maneuver, so startle is missing; UPRT aims at unplanned excursions [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

cards.s: Under the FAA definition, an upset can include an overspeed, not just a stall.
cards.why: True. Upsets include stalls and overspeeds or other inappropriate speeds [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

cards.s: Many upsets happen while the pilot is busy with a task that takes attention away from the instruments or the outside view.

activities.title: Name the human factor
activities.intro: Tap a term, then the description that fits it.

pairs.r: An unexpected event that breaks your expectations and disrupts your thinking
An automatic muscle reflex with a jump in heart rate and blood pressure
The task demands more than you can give, so the margin of safety is gone
Many lights, sounds and shakes arrive at once and are hard to sort
Setting the avionics or chasing a malfunction pulls you off basic control

activities.why: Surprise, startle, task saturation and sensory overload [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Diversion of attention [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

activities.title: Work the lift, ice and altitude numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: AC 61-67C reports stall speed increases as high as 50 knots seen after icing upsets. For an airplane with a clean stall speed of 48 knots, by about what percent would a 50 knot increase raise the stall speed? (whole number)
items.why: 50 / 48 = 1.042, about a 104 percent increase, more than double the clean stall speed (48 + 50 = 98 knots) [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102b]]. Contamination can make the airplane stall at much higher speeds than normal [[28:249|AWH 20.3.10]].

items.q: A 2,300 lb airplane is in a level, coordinated 60 degree bank. How much lift must the wings produce?
items.why: A level 60 degree bank is 2 G, and the wing must produce lift equal to the load factor times the weight to hold altitude [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C par 100g]]: 2 x 2,300 = 4,600 lb.

items.q: Over a town, the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft of you is a 380 ft tower standing on ground at 900 ft MSL. What is the lowest altitude 91.119 allows (ft MSL)?
items.why: Over a congested area, fly 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a 2,000 ft radius [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. The tower top is 900 + 380 = 1,280 ft MSL, plus 1,000 = 2,280 ft MSL.

items.q: The PHAK says more than 25 percent of GA fatal accidents happen in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve a stall or spin. Out of 400 fatal accidents, at least about how many are maneuvering stall or spin accidents?
items.why: 400 x 0.25 = 100 in maneuvering, and half of 100 is 50 [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]]. Since the share is more than 25 percent, the true number is a bit higher.

activities.title: How the base-to-final skid becomes a spin
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the chain of events in order, then tap Check.
steps: An unnoticed tailwind on base gives a higher groundspeed
The pilot turns late or too shallow and overshoots the centerline
The pilot steepens the bank, adds back pressure and pushes inside rudder
The bank keeps growing and the nose slices below the horizon
The pilot pulls harder and the AOA nears critical
The airplane stalls with crossed controls and can quickly enter a spin
activities.why: This is the AFH's skidding cross-control stall chain; the safest fix at the overshoot step is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

activities.title: Back in the air, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying again after three years away. You rent a four-seat single with a new GPS and an autopilot you have used only once. Solo, VFR, you are climbing out toward 5,500 ft with the autopilot holding pitch.

steps.s: Head down programming the unfamiliar GPS, you look up: the airspeed is far below the climb speed and the stall warning sounds. First action?
options: Use the autopilot's pitch wheel to lower the nose
Add full power and leave the autopilot on
Roll into a turn to look for traffic
steps.why: Step one of the stall recovery template is to disconnect, since the autopilot may make control or trim changes you will not notice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Setting avionics is a known diversion of attention [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

steps.s: With the autopilot off, the yoke pulls back hard: it had trimmed far nose-up. What now?
options: Let the nose rise while you add power
Push to lower the nose until the warning stops, and trim nose-down as needed
steps.why: Pitch nose-down until the impending stall cues are gone, using nose-down trim if needed [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. A sudden disconnect with the trim at an extreme setting complicates the recovery [[13:10|AC 61-67C par 102c]].

steps.s: The warning has stopped, but the left wing is down about 20 degrees. Next?
options: Roll the wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder
Pull back to stop the descent
Full right aileron with no rudder
steps.why: After the AOA is reduced, roll wings level and use rudder to stop any yaw so the stall does not become a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: Wings level, power up, speed building. You are 300 ft below where you were. What now?
options: Pull up sharply to get the altitude back
Return smoothly to the desired flightpath, avoiding a secondary stall
Re-engage the autopilot and go back to the GPS
Climb at the slowest speed you can hold
steps.why: Return with smooth, coordinated inputs, careful to avoid a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]; an abrupt pull-up after recovery is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

steps.s: Later, over dark water at dusk, the horizon fades. You find the airspeed climbing fast, the altimeter unwinding and a steep bank. What do you do?
options: Pull back firmly while rolling level
Power to idle, unload with some forward elevator, roll wings level, then raise the nose gently
Full opposite rudder and forward elevator
Add power and pull to climb
steps.why: Rising airspeed means a spiral dive, not a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Idle, unload to about 1 G, roll level, then gently raise the nose; a rolling pullout can exceed the design limit [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
